q: In 1896, ____ discovered that uranium salts emit radiations which affect photographic plates and cause ionization.
e: Henry Becquerel was the first to discover radioactivity in uranium salts.

q: The radiations are emitted from the ____ of uranium atoms and are of three types; namely alpha, beta and gamma rays.
e: Radioactive emissions originate from the unstable nucleus of an atom.

q: Hence, the emission of some or all of alpha, beta and gamma rays from the nucleus of an unstable atom is called ____.
e: Radioactivity is the phenomenon of spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable nuclei.

q: The term radioactivity is also known as radioactive decay, radioactive disintegration, nuclear decay, or ____.
e: These terms all describe the process by which an unstable atomic nucleus loses energy by radiation.

q: Of all 92 elements which exist in nature, only a few heavy elements with atomic number greater than ____ are radioactive or unstable.
e: Elements with atomic numbers above 83 (Bismuth) are naturally radioactive.

q: Some examples of radioactive elements (or radioactive substances) are uranium, thorium, radium, polonium and radon; of which radium and polonium were discovered by ____.
e: Marie Curie discovered radium and polonium through her pioneering research on radioactivity.

q: Radioactive elements can also be artificially produced using nuclear reactors and ____.
e: Particle accelerators and nuclear reactors are used to create artificial radioisotopes.

q:
$ eta^-$ decay (beta-minus decay) is a process in which a ____ in an atomic nucleus changes to a proton with the emission of an electron ($ eta^-$) and an antineutrino ($ ar{
u}_e$).
e: In beta-minus decay, a neutron converts into a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino.

q: In $ eta^-$ decay, the parent nucleus transforms into the daughter nucleus, with mass number remains unchanged but atomic number ____ by one.
e: Because a neutron becomes a proton, the atomic number increases by one while the mass number stays the same.

q:
$ eta^+$ decay (beta-plus decay) is a process in which a proton in an atomic nucleus changes to a neutron with the emission of a ____ ($ eta^+$) and a neutrino ($
u_e$).
e: Beta-plus decay involves the emission of a positron, which is the antimatter counterpart of an electron.

q: In $ eta^+$ decay, the parent nucleus transforms into the daughter nucleus, with mass number remains unchanged but atomic number ____ by one.
e: Since a proton converts into a neutron, the atomic number decreases by one.

q: Positron, the ____ of electron, has the same mass and same magnitude of electric charge as an electron; but positron is positively charged.
e: The positron is the antiparticle of the electron, possessing identical mass but opposite charge.

q: The existence of positron was theoretically predicted by Dirac in 1931 and experimentally detected by ____ in 1932.
e: Carl Anderson experimentally confirmed the existence of the positron in cosmic ray experiments.

q: Neutrino, a fundamental particle as an electron, has ____ and negligibly small rest mass.
e: Neutrinos are electrically neutral fundamental particles with extremely small mass.

q: For a nucleus to be stable, there must be an appropriate ____ of protons and neutrons.
e: Nuclear stability depends heavily on the specific ratio of neutrons to protons in the nucleus.

q: If a nucleus has ____, $ eta^-$ decay takes place.
e: Nuclei with too many neutrons undergo beta-minus decay to convert a neutron into a proton.

q: Conversely, a nucleus with ____ undergoes $ eta^+$ decay.
e: Nuclei with too many protons undergo beta-plus decay to convert a proton into a neutron.

q: In gamma decay, the atomic number and mass number of the parent and daughter nuclei remain ____.
e: Gamma decay only releases energy; it does not change the number of protons or neutrons.

q: The photon is the ____ of the electromagnetic field including electromagnetic radiation such as light, X-rays and gamma rays.
e: A photon is the fundamental particle or quantum of electromagnetic radiation.

q: Photons are ____ and move at the speed of light in vacuum.
e: Photons have zero rest mass, allowing them to travel at the speed of light.

q: The energy of a photon is ____ proportional to the wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation associated with it.
e: According to Planck's equation, shorter wavelengths correspond to higher photon energies.

q: Alpha rays consist of ____, positively charged particles.
e: Alpha particles are identical to helium-4 nuclei, containing two protons and two neutrons.

q: Alpha rays are the ____ ionizing of the three rays.
e: Due to their large mass and double positive charge, alpha particles strongly interact with matter and cause high ionization.

q: Alpha rays are the ____ penetrating of the three rays.
e: Their strong ionizing power causes them to lose energy quickly, resulting in very low penetration depth.

q: Alpha rays can be stopped by a thick sheet of ____.
e: Alpha particles have such low penetrating power that even a sheet of paper can block them.

q: Beta rays consists of either electrons (charge $=-e$) or ____ (charge $= +e$) moving with varying speeds.
e: Beta radiation can be composed of beta-minus (electrons) or beta-plus (positrons) particles.

q: Beta rays can be stopped by a few millimetres of ____.
e: Beta particles have moderate penetrating power and are typically stopped by a thin sheet of aluminum.

q: Gamma rays are electromagnetic waves like light and X-rays, but have much ____ wavelengths.
e: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths and highest frequencies in the electromagnetic spectrum.

q: Gamma rays cannot be deflected by electric and ____ fields.
e: Because gamma rays are uncharged photons, they do not interact with electric or magnetic fields.

q: Intensity of gamma rays can be greatly reduced by several centimetres of ____ but they are never completely stopped.
e: Dense materials like lead or thick concrete are required to significantly attenuate gamma radiation.

q: The rate of decay of a radioactive sample is called ____.
e: Activity measures the number of disintegrations occurring in a radioactive sample per unit time.

q: SI unit for activity is ____ (Bq).
e: One becquerel is defined as one radioactive decay or disintegration per second.

q: The rate of decay (activity) is a characteristic of the radioactive element and it is unaffected by the ____.
e: Radioactive decay is a nuclear process and is independent of external physical conditions like temperature or pressure.

q: The half-life is defined as the time for ____ the atoms in a radioactive sample to decay.
e: Half-life is the time required for exactly 50% of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to undergo decay.

q: Radioactive decay is a ____ process: it is impossible to predict when a particular atom will decay, regardless of how long the atom has existed.
e: While individual decay events are random and unpredictable, the overall behavior of a large sample follows statistical laws.

q: A radioisotope (radioactive isotope or radionuclide) is an atom with an ____ nucleus which undergoes radioactive decay.
e: Radioisotopes possess unstable nuclei that spontaneously emit radiation to achieve a more stable state.

q: A ____ is a small amount of radioactive isotope introduced into a system in order to follow the behaviour of some components of that system.
e: Radioactive tracers are used in medicine and industry to track the movement or distribution of substances.

q: In medicine, radioactive tracers are effectively used in diagnostic procedures, for example, to check ____ function using radioactive iodine-131.
e: The thyroid gland naturally absorbs iodine, making iodine-131 an ideal tracer for diagnosing thyroid conditions.

q: For medical tests, artificial radioisotopes with ____ half-lives are used so that there is no detectable radiation after a few days.
e: Short half-lives minimize the patient's radiation exposure while allowing enough time for diagnostic imaging.

q: Treatment with radiation is known as ____.
e: Radiotherapy uses targeted ionizing radiation to destroy cancer cells and shrink tumors.

q: In industrial ____ radiography, radioactive materials are used to inspect metal castings or welded joints.
e: Industrial gamma radiography functions similarly to medical X-rays to find internal flaws in metal structures.

q: Radioactive dating is a technique for estimating the ____ of an object by measuring the amounts of various radioisotopes present in it.
e: By measuring the ratio of parent to daughter isotopes, scientists can calculate the age of geological or biological samples.

q: Carbon dating is a technique for estimating the age of the remains of plants and animals by measuring the activity of ____ presents in the remains.
e: Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope incorporated into living organisms, which decays at a known rate after death.

q: Carbon-14 is continually produced by ____ entering the upper atmosphere.
e: High-energy cosmic rays strike the atmosphere, generating neutrons that convert nitrogen into carbon-14.

q: When rocks are formed, some radioisotopes become trapped in them, for example, ____ is trapped in igneous rocks.
e: Potassium-40 is commonly used in radioactive dating to determine the age of igneous rock formations.

q: Gamma and neutron irradiation of seeds can be used to induce ____ to develop desired mutants that are resistant to disease.
e: Controlled radiation induces genetic mutations in agriculture to breed crops with beneficial traits.
